title: Chicago’s bid to lead the country in quantum computing
content: Quantum Research Blog Chicago’s bid to lead the country in quantum computing New IBM Quantum System Two supports Illinois’ place at the center of the American quantum computing industry. Date 6 Nov 2026 Authors Rafi Letzter Topics Network Community Systems Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key Takeaways: IBM has deployed an IBM Quantum System Two with an IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor at the University of Chicago's Hyde Park Labs to support the National Quantum Algorithm Center (NQAC) and the wider Illinois quantum ecosystem. IBM is an anchor partner of the NQAC in Chicago, which was created by the State of Illinois in concert with the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP). IQMP will be a quantum computing campus on the former US Steel South Works site on Chicago's Southeast Side, and will eventually house the new computer and NQAC. The IBM Quantum System Two sits at street level behind floor-to-ceiling windows at Hyde Park Labs on 53rd Street. IQMP CEO Harley T. Johnson calls it "probably the most publicly visible quantum computer in the world." The University of Illinois, University of Chicago, and other key research and business institutions in the region are already conducting important research that advances quantum computing as a technology, science, and industry. Johnson and Mason emphasize that Illinois' quantum leadership is rooted in decades of investment in scientific and engineering talent. Across the Midwest, universities, national laboratories, and technology companies have helped develop generations of researchers, engineers, and entrepreneurs. Harley T. Johnson wants Chicago to be the Silicon Valley of quantum computing. Johnson is a professor of mechanical science and engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (U of I.) and CEO of the Illinois Quantum and Microelectronics Park (IQMP). He is part of a cohort of leaders spanning academia, government, and industry who are working to establish Chicago as the hub of America’s quantum computing industry. That effort has a physical center. With a $500 million investment from the state of Illinois under Governor JB Pritzker, as well as support from IBM, U of I., the University of Chicago, and other partner organizations, the IQMP will be a massive campus on a pier that once housed a U.S. Steel South Works plant on Chicago’s Southeast Side. As part of that project, the state established the National Quantum Algorithm Center (NQAC), a Chicago-based collaborative initiative focused on advancing quantum algorithms and applications to support the emerging quantum computing industry. IBM is an anchor partner. To support the algorithm center and surrounding quantum ecosystem, IBM has unveiled a newly installed IBM Quantum System Two with an IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processor at UChicago’s Hyde Park Labs. The system will operate at UChicago before eventually relocating to the IQMP campus, which will serve as the long-term home of both the NQAC and the new quantum computer. Pritzker and Johnson joined a group of Illinois leaders for the ribbon cutting including UChicago President Paul Alivisatos, Chairman of the Illinois Economic Development Corporation John Atkinson, Assistant Director and Chief Workforce Officer of the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity Stacia Edwards, P33 CEO Brad Henderson, U of I. Chancellor Charles Isbell, and UChicago Vice President of Research Nadya Mason. IBM Director of Research Jay Gambetta, and Director of Quantum Algorithm Centers Hanhee Paik stood with them to unveil the quantum computer at a ceremony on November 6. Mason has been a researcher and leader in the quantum field for decades and has played a key role in building Chicago’s quantum ecosystem. She said that the arrival of the IBM Quantum System Two will accelerate the work and increase the excitement for quantum computing that’s already taken root in the region. Johnson said it’s important to him that the computer will have such a prominent location in the city. “It’s probably the most publicly visible quantum computer in the world,” Johnson said. Sitting at ground level behind floor-to-ceiling windows at Hyde Park Labs on 53rd Street, the mirrored panels of the IBM Quantum System Two will reflect the faces of students from the public high school just a block away as they walk past and peer through the glass. "Imagine getting to say, ‘My daughter goes to school every day and passes a real quantum computer.’ That’s mind blowing,” Johnson said. Already, Mason said, adults are getting inspired by the possibilities the new quantum computer represents. “For our graduate students, having access to a quantum computer is incredible,” she said. There are many students and researchers in the Pritzker School of Engineering at UChicago with deep expertise in quantum information science and engineering.
